Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

Today we'll continue with module 5 on energy storage devices that is on fuel cells.

Key details

  • This fuel cell is also known as proton exchange membrane fuel cells, thus telling us that the polymer which we are going to use is capable of exchanging protons.
  • Why is methanol fuel cell so popular these days.
  • If you remember in the hydrogen oxygen fuel cell I mentioned that storage and transport of hydrogen is going to be difficult because it is in the form of a gas.
  • But methanol being a liquid.
  • We can easily transport and store the methanol, and hence there is a possibility that we can use it for portable devices.
  • This fuel cell has low weight and volume.
  • Low weight and volume because we are we are using polymer as the electrolyte and polymers are lightweight.
  • So therefore this cell will have very low weight and volume and therefore.
  • What is the good characteristic of this fuel cell?
  • That it is going to have very high energy density.
  • The weight has reduced, therefore the energy density will be very high.
  • But there is one problem we face with this fuel cell, that we have to use only noble metal as catalyst, and usually it is platinum which is employed as the catalyst in these cells.
  • And one more problem which we face that carbon monoxide.
  • If it is present, then it is going to poison the catalyst.
  • We are using platinum as the catalyst.
  • It is going to poison the catalyst, and therefore pure fuel or oxidant only should be used.
  • The electrode is a porous carbon electrode containing platinum.
  • Cathode is also a porous carbon electrode containing platinum.
  • Just now I mentioned that noble metal only should be used, but then we always have to have a porous electrode.
  • because all reactions are going to take place on the electrode.
  • The catalyst is present there, the electrolyte is in contact, and also the fuel or the oxidant is going to come in contact with the electrode.
  • It is a solution of methanol.
  • We never use pure methanol.
  • We are going to use a solution of methanol and the oxidant is oxygen gas.
  • of methanol and the oxidant is a oxygen is the oxygen gas and the electrolyte as we are studying now it is a proton conducting polymer membrane now any electrolyte for that matter.
  • What should be the criteria that it has to be an electronic insulator?
  • What does it mean?
  • That it is not going to allow the electrons to move through itself that is the electrolyte should be an electronic insulator.
  • Yes, we are using a polymer here, so this membrane is an electronic insulator, but at the same time we want the hydrogen ions to move.
  • That's why we have chosen a proton exchange membrane.

Excellent conductor of the hydrogen ions.

Key details

  • Electrolyte is usually the most common electrolyte used is a fluorocarbon backbone.
  • It's similar to Teflon.

  • It becomes like this in the presence of water.
  • The H plus ions obviously are going to be able to migrate through when the membrane is hydrated.
  • So when because when it is hydrated, you will be able to get the H plus ions to move through the electrolyte.
  • The most common one in any protonic stain membrane electrolyte fuel cell or we can call it as a polymer electrolyte fuel cell.

  • As I said, there's a backbone of CF2, and then that is the Teflon backbone, and then here we see the SO3H groups which have been appended onto this backbone.
  • is acquebn which also has a similar structure just that the CF2 branching I mean the CF2 chain has been reduced.
  • Here it is a longer chain and here you can see it's a smaller chain.

  • Direct methanol fuel cells.

  • Here you can see the methanol diffuses through the membrane to the cathode.
  • So instead of reacting at the anode undergoing oxidation at the anode we find that methanol just crosses over to the cathode and there it is going to combine with the oxygen which is not what we want because if we want to generate power from the cell then oxidation of methanol has to happen at the anode but.
  • But unfortunately, when we use Nafion, it is found that this methanol crossover happens.
  • So, therefore, that will result in what you will get lower voltage because less number of electrons are being generated.

Core explanation · 15:00–19:59

This is called water management.

Key details

  • Now when we have high temperature, what is the problem if we use high temperature what will happen the polymer may get dehydrated and therefore H plus conductivity cannot take place and also the polymer may degrade and crack resulting in short circuiting.
  • And another reason for this, another fact which we have to know is that.
  • Neither can low temperatures be used because this will result in flooding the cell because water will not be removed if you keep it at a very low temperature.
  • Water will not be removed and this will result in flooding of the cell and that reduces the efficiency of the cell.
  • And also because the temperature is very low, we will require a higher loading of catalyst.
  • We are using platinum as the catalyst.
  • we have we it will be very expensive.
  • Neither can we use a high temperature, neither can we use a low temperature.
  • What are the advantages of this fuel cell?
  • So as mentioned it is it has a very high energy density because of the low weight of the polymer.
  • And then it has a long life because we are using work making it work at a very low temperature and therefore the with low temperature it will start very quickly.
  • first of all, and it also results in less wear and tear of the system components and therefore a better durability.
  • No free corrosive liquid is being used in the cell because the electrolyte is a polymer.
  • Therefore, there is no free corrosive liquid which is being used in the cell.
  • Noble metal catalysts have to be used and the electrolyte is also expensive.
  • We are using special electrolytes, special proton exchange membranes have to be used.
  • And if we have CO then carbon monoxide if at all present it is going to poison the platinum catalyst and hence pure reactant should be.
  • And management of carbon dioxide, which is created at the anode and water management pose problems.
  • As I mentioned that water shouldn't be present in a right amount, when in the right amount and it should not be in excess.
  • just now we discussed water management.

  • fuel cell using solid oxide as the electrolyte.
